ar.accuracy.calibrate: The compass needs calibrating. Move the phone in a figure of eight, and stand clear of metal, magnets and car dashboards.
ar.accuracy.note: The figure at the top of the frame is the heading accuracy the device reports. The positions themselves are computed, not measured, and are accurate to far better than the compass can be aimed.

ar.camera.restricted: The camera is restricted on this device, so the paths are drawn over the sky colour instead. Everything else on this screen still works.
ar.camera.unavailable: There is no camera here, so the paths are drawn over the sky colour instead. Everything else on this screen still works.

ar.milkyWay.notDark: The Milky Way is drawn once the sun is more than eighteen degrees below the horizon. It is not dark enough at the selected time.
ar.moon.locked: The moon is part of Sunlit Pro: its path over your view, its phase, and its rise and set with parallax.

ar.sweep.explanation: Aim the centre of the frame at the top of whatever blocks your view, then hold Sweep and turn on the spot. The sky is divided into thirty six sectors of ten degrees and each one fills as you reach it.
ar.sweep.locked: Sweeping your skyline is part of Sunlit Pro. It gives you the sunrise and sunset your own surroundings actually produce, and the periods when the sun is up but behind them.

credits.methods.detail: Every figure in Sunlit is computed on your device from published algorithms. No server is ever asked for a sun, moon or sky figure, and nothing about you is collected or sent. Two things do use the network, both of them Apple's and neither of them a calculation: the map tiles in the Map view, and the time zone of a pin you drop somewhere new.
credits.models.detail: The UV index and the irradiance figures are clear sky models. They say what the sky would deliver with no cloud, no haze and no pollution, from your latitude, the date and the sun's height. They are not measurements, Sunlit has no sensor for either, and real weather can put them far off.
credits.places.detail: The offline city list is the GeoNames cities15000 extract: every populated place above fifteen thousand people, with its coordinate, elevation and time zone. It is used under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence, and it is stored in the app so that search works with no network.
credits.title: Data and methods
credits.trueNorth.detail: The AR view takes its direction from the device's true north reference frame, computed by iOS from the compass, the gyroscope and your position. Sunlit does not correct it further, and it shows the current uncertainty on screen instead of hiding it.
data.annual.belowHorizon: Where the curve runs under the horizon line the sun does not rise at all on that date.
data.annual.caption: The highest the sun reaches on each date of the year at this place. The four light uprights are the equinoxes and the solstices. The heavier one is the date you have selected, which is a fifth upright on all but those four dates.
data.annual.spreadCaption: The difference between the highest and the lowest the midday sun gets here. Outside the tropics it is about forty seven degrees, twice the tilt of the earth. Inside them it is less, because the noon sun passes overhead twice a year and turns back.
data.annual.title: The sun across the year
data.card.footer: Computed on device by Sunlit. UV index is a clear sky model.
data.context.subtitle: \(day). All times in \(zoneName).
data.eclipse.alreadyUnderWay: The sun rises here with the eclipse already in progress, so there is no first contact to see.
data.eclipse.caption: The next solar eclipse visible from this place, and the next lunar eclipse wherever it falls, searched over the coming five years. A lunar eclipse happens at the same instant everywhere on Earth, so one is listed even when the moon is below the horizon here. All times are local to this place.
data.eclipse.lowSun: The sun is close to the horizon then, so you will need a clear view in that direction.
data.eclipse.magnitudeCaption: How much of the sun's diameter the moon covers at maximum, as a share of that diameter. It passes one when the moon's disc is the larger of the two.
data.eclipse.moonBelowHorizon: The moon is below the horizon here at maximum, so this eclipse happens while it is out of sight from this place. The contact times are the same everywhere on Earth; only whether you can see them changes.
data.eclipse.noLunar: No lunar eclipse falls anywhere in the next five years.
data.eclipse.noMaximum: No part of this eclipse happens while the sun is above the horizon here.
data.eclipse.noSolar: No solar eclipse is visible from this place in the next five years.
data.eclipse.obscurationCaption: Fraction of the sun's area covered at maximum. Never larger than the magnitude, because a bite taken out of the edge of a disc removes less of its area than of its width.
data.eclipse.phaseAbsent: This eclipse does not reach that phase.
data.eclipse.sunSetFirst: The sun sets here before the discs part, so there is no last contact to see.
data.eclipse.title: Eclipses
data.eclipse.umbralCaption: How much of the moon's diameter is inside the dark shadow at maximum, as a share of that diameter. Above one the whole moon is inside it. Below zero the moon misses the umbra altogether.
data.eclipse.waiting: The next eclipses will be searched for shortly.
data.export.caption: A spreadsheet of every figure on this screen, and a picture of the day to send on.
data.export.csvDetail: One row per figure, with a header row, the unit it is expressed in, and a note wherever a value is absent that says why.
data.export.failed: This file could not be written on this device.
data.export.imageDetail: The day's headline figures on the sky colour of its own solar noon.

data.export.zoneExplanation: Every time in both files is written for \(name), with its offset from Universal Time attached. The spreadsheet is in English with ISO 8601 timestamps and a full stop as the decimal separator, so that anyone can open it.
data.footer.offline: Every figure here is computed on this device from the selected place and date. Nothing on this screen needs a network.
data.golden.caption: Golden is the sun between four degrees below and six degrees above the horizon. Blue is between six and four degrees below it. Neither is an hour.
data.golden.noCrossing: The sun does not cross this band on this side of solar noon.
data.golden.staysAbove: The sun stays above this band all day here, so there is no window.
data.golden.staysBelow: The sun stays below this band all day here, so there is no window.
data.golden.title: Golden and blue hour

data.milkyWay.caption: The galactic centre above ten degrees, the sun below eighteen degrees, and no bright moon up. For the night that begins on this date.
data.milkyWay.highestCaption: The highest the galactic centre reached at any point in the night, whether or not the sky was dark then.
data.milkyWay.limit.belowHorizon: The galactic centre never rises ten degrees above the horizon from this place on this night. It climbs highest from around twenty nine degrees south, where it passes overhead, and sits lower from anywhere further north or further south of that.
data.milkyWay.limit.moonlight: A bright moon is above the horizon through every dark hour of this night. Wait for a thinner moon.
data.milkyWay.limit.season: The galactic centre is high, and the night is dark, but never at the same time. This is the wrong half of the year at this latitude.
data.milkyWay.limit.twilight: The sun never sinks eighteen degrees below the horizon on this night, so the sky never becomes astronomically dark. This is the high latitude summer, whichever hemisphere you are in.
data.milkyWay.limit.unknown: There is no window on the galactic centre on this night.
data.milkyWay.title: Milky Way
data.model.clearSky: UV index and irradiance are clear sky models, not measurements. They assume a cloudless atmosphere.
data.model.clearSkyShort: Clear sky model, not a measurement
data.moon.alwaysDown: The moon stays below the horizon all day here.
data.moon.alwaysUp: The moon stays above the horizon all day here.
data.moon.caption: Phase, illumination and distance at local noon. Rise and set account for the moon's parallax, which makes it sit almost a degree lower than it would seen from the centre of the earth, so moonrise falls later than a flat calculation gives.
data.moon.noRiseToday: The moon does not rise on this date. It rises about fifty minutes later each day, so roughly once a month a date has no moonrise in it at all.
data.moon.noSetToday: The moon does not set on this date. It sets about fifty minutes later each day, so roughly once a month a date has no moonset in it at all.
data.moon.title: Moon
data.sun.noAzimuth: There is no event to take an azimuth from on this date.
data.sun.noSunrise: The sun does not cross the horizon upward on this date.
data.sun.noSunset: The sun does not cross the horizon downward on this date.
data.sun.noTransit: The sun does not cross the meridian above the horizon on this date.
data.sun.polarDay: The sun stays above the horizon all day here, so there is no sunrise and no sunset on this date.
data.sun.polarNight: The sun stays below the horizon all day here, so there is no sunrise and no sunset on this date.
data.sun.title: Sun
data.terrain.caption: Compared against the skyline you swept here, not against a flat horizon.
data.terrain.neverClears: The sun does not clear your skyline at all on this date.
data.terrain.noDifference: The same as a flat horizon
data.terrain.noFlatEvent: There is no flat horizon event on this date to compare against.
data.terrain.noObstruction: Your skyline does not block the sun at any point on this date.
data.terrain.notMeasured: No skyline has been swept for this place yet. Sweep one in the AR view and this table fills in with the times your own surroundings block the sun.
data.terrain.title: Skyline
data.twilight.astronomical.neverDark: The sun does not sink eighteen degrees below the horizon on this date, so the night never becomes astronomically dark.
data.twilight.astronomical.neverLight: The sun stays more than eighteen degrees below the horizon all day here. It is astronomically dark throughout.
data.twilight.caption: Civil at six degrees, nautical at twelve, astronomical at eighteen degrees below the horizon.
data.twilight.civil.neverDark: The sun does not sink six degrees below the horizon on this date, so civil twilight lasts all night.
data.twilight.civil.neverLight: The sun stays more than six degrees below the horizon all day here, so civil twilight does not begin.
data.twilight.nautical.neverDark: The sun does not sink twelve degrees below the horizon on this date, so nautical twilight lasts all night.
data.twilight.nautical.neverLight: The sun stays more than twelve degrees below the horizon all day here, so nautical twilight does not begin.
data.twilight.noCrossing: The sun does not cross this boundary on this side of the day.
data.twilight.title: Twilight

map.networkNotice: Apple serves the map tiles over the network. Every azimuth, time and length here is worked out on your device and needs no connection. The one thing looked up over the network is a dropped pin's own time zone, and the note at the top of this panel says when that lookup has not answered.
map.noMoonEvent: The moon neither rises nor sets on this day here, so it is either above the horizon for the whole day or below it for the whole day. Both events run about fifty minutes later each day, so a calendar day can fall between one pair of them and the next.
map.polarDay: The sun stays above the horizon all day here, so there is no sunrise or sunset to point at.
map.polarNight: The sun stays below the horizon all day here, so there is no sunrise or sunset to point at.
map.shadow.clamped: The shadow runs further than the drawn line, which stops at \(limit). The length above is the whole of it.
map.shadow.levelGround: Exact geometry on level ground. The map does not know what the shadow falls on, or what stands in its way.
map.shadow.none: The sun is below the horizon at this instant, so there is no shadow to draw.
map.tapHint: Tap the map to move the pin. Press and hold to drop one and centre on it. Every other view follows the pin.
